ann_119.original: The gate is a ReLU of capital gains with a small born-in-Portugal term, both in z units (formula attached as analytical_formula evidence; the rounded closed form is off from the exact node by up to 0.0058); its output enters the logit with weight -2.32, the same direction as the direct capital-gains edge (weight -2.49 per sd). Hypothesis: once capital gains pass a threshold the model adds a second, steeper push towards a high income on top of the direct capital-gains edge. For the typical person the gate is still shut at 4630 US dollars and open at 4640 US dollars. At 10000 US dollars it adds -0.96 to the logit, so the predicted chance of a low income is 2% with the gate and 6% without it. In the training data it acts on 2094 people (mean contribution -2.51 on the logit for them; their low-income rate is 13.7%). Outside the Portugal-born, the gate is off for 0 people with gains of 4650 dollars or more and on for 0 people with less. The Portugal term is kept because it matters for that group: for a Portugal-born typical person the gate is still shut at 20000 US dollars and opens only by 40000 US dollars; of the 49 Portugal-born training people, 0 have the gate on, and 1 of them has gains above the usual threshold yet keeps it shut. Switching the gate off moves the training AUC from 0.9099 to 0.9093: a small loss, because the direct edge already separates most high earners.
ann_119.proposed: Above about 4507 US dollars of capital gains this switch lowers the predicted chance of a low income further; for a typical person it acts on, from about 4% without it to about 2% with it.

ann_120.original: A hinge on age with a handlers-or-cleaners term (formula attached as analytical_formula evidence, z units; the rounded closed form is off from the exact node by up to 0.0062). Its output enters the logit with weight 0.67, towards a low income. Hypothesis: the model treats youth as a strong sign of a low income and, past the hinge, almost ignores age. For the typical person the hinge is open at 34 years and shut at 35 years; at 20 years it adds 2.05 to the logit (predicted chance of a low income 93%, against 65% without the hinge). Above the hinge only the direct age edge is left (weight -0.06 per sd), so in the whole model the typical person's predicted chance moves only from 63% at 35 years to 62% at 45 years. Partner: being a handler or cleaner moves the hinge to older ages; for a typical handler or cleaner it is still open at 43 years and shut at 44 years. In the training data the hinge is open for 17,107 people (low-income rate 89.5%, mean contribution 1.25 on the logit for them); it is open for all 14,746 people aged 32 or younger (0 of them have it shut) and for 1310 people aged 34 or older. Switching it off moves the training AUC from 0.9099 to 0.9039, the second-largest loss of any part.
ann_120.proposed: Youth raises the predicted chance of a low income: through this switch a typical person goes from about 91% at 22 years to about 63% at 58 years, with no further change past about 34 years.

ann_121.original: A two-unit chain read from the White race indicator alone (formula attached as analytical_formula evidence, z units; the rounded closed form is off from the exact node by up to 0.0026). Its output enters the logit with weight 0.76. Hypothesis: it is a two-valued lookup that gives White people a fixed push towards a low income, which offsets part of the direct race edges pushing the other way. Self-probe over every race level for the typical person: the chain's output is 1.066 for White and 0.0 for American Indian or Eskimo, 0.0 for Asian or Pacific Islander, 0.0 for Black and 0.0 for other race. In the training data it is on for the 33,425 White people; 0 White people have it off and 0 non-White people have it on. For a typical White person it adds 0.81 to the logit, while the direct terms sum to -1.48 for White against -0.36 for Black (the direct White edge alone weighs -0.40 per sd). In the whole model the typical person's predicted chance of a low income is 63% as White and 70% as Black. Switching the chain off moves the training AUC from 0.9099 to 0.9083. Being a function of one indicator, it could be folded into the direct White edge; the chain and the edge together set the model's race offset for White people.
ann_121.proposed: A fixed push towards a low income for White people: through it a typical person of another race gets about 43% rather than about 63%.

ann_122.original: A gate over occupation, doctorate, work-without-pay and born-in-Colombia indicators, with two small inner units (formula attached as analytical_formula evidence, z units; the rounded closed form is off from the exact node by up to 0.0058). Its output enters the logit with weight 0.24, towards a low income. Hypothesis: the model gives a fixed push towards a low income to almost everyone, and withholds it from executives or managers, members of the armed forces, farmers or fishers, doctorate holders and people working without pay; being born in Colombia reopens the gate with a very large push. Self-probe over every occupation for the typical person: the gate's output is 1.21 for administrative or clerical work (adding 0.29 to the logit), 1.54 for sales, and 0.0, 0.0 and 0.0 for executive or managerial, armed forces and farming or fishing. A doctorate also shuts it (0.0, against 1.21 for a high-school graduate), and so does working without pay (0.0). For a typical executive born in Colombia the output is 39.2 and the predicted chance of a low income above 99%, against 56% for one born in the United States. In the training data the gate is open for 32,617 people and shut for 6456. Of the 6046 people in the three occupations, 4 have it open, and 4 of those were born in Colombia; of the 473 doctorate holders, 0 have it open; outside the three occupations and the doctorates, 11 people have it shut, and 11 of them work without pay. The Colombia term is fitted to 64 Colombia-born training people: for them the gate adds 10.3 to the logit on average, their mean predicted chance of a low income is 1.000 and their observed rate 98.4%. Switching the gate off moves the training AUC from 0.9099 to 0.9092.
ann_122.proposed: A push towards a low income for most occupations, raising a typical person's predicted chance from about 66% to about 72%, held back for executives or managers, farmers or fishers and doctorate holders, and very large for people born in Colombia (above 99%).

ann_130.original: The direct input-to-output edges, gathered in one identity node: a weighted sum of the z-scored inputs (the full sum is attached as analytical_formula evidence; the rounded closed form is off from the exact node by up to 0.034 on a node whose training range spans 38.5). Hypothesis: this linear score carries most of the model's ranking: higher capital gains, capital losses, schooling and weekly hours, and being married, each move the prediction towards a high income in proportion to the input. The heaviest edges per sd are capital gains -2.49, married to a civilian spouse -1.19, not living in a family -0.85, husband -0.75, education-num -0.56, wife -0.56, unmarried -0.54, hours per week -0.31, sex (male) -0.31 and capital losses -0.27. Because the one-hot indicators are z-scored, a category's effect is the difference between two levels' edges, not one weight. Self-probe of linearity for the typical person: the direct sum is -0.983, -1.483 and -1.982 at 20 hours, 40 hours and 60 hours (equal steps), and -0.615, -1.483 and -2.351 at education levels 5 on the 1-16 scale, 9 on the 1-16 scale and 13 on the 1-16 scale; the predicted chance of a low income falls from 80% to 42% over that range. Capital losses lower it too: 63% at 0 US dollars and 31% at 2000 US dollars. Marital status moves it most among the categories: with everything else held at the typical (married, husband) case, setting marital status to never married moves the direct sum from -1.48 to 0.90 and the predicted chance from 63% to 95%. For a never-married person not in a family, being a man lowers the predicted chance from 96% to 92%. Setting the whole direct sum to its training mean drops the training AUC from 0.9099 to 0.7093, by far the largest loss of any part.
ann_130.proposed: A direct sum of every input: for a typical person, capital gains of 6849 US dollars bring the predicted chance of a low income from about 63% to about 15%, a professional school degree to about 19%, and being a woman raises it to about 96%.

ann_131.original: Composition of six parallel children, added side by side at the output: the White and the Asian or Pacific Islander race chains, the other-service unit, the seventh-to-eighth-grade unit, the Hungary unit and the eleventh-grade unit. Its contribution is the sum of the children's. Hypothesis: each of the six children takes a single category indicator as its entry, so each is a two-valued offset for one category (on the data, a correction to that indicator's direct edge, or the whole of that indicator's effect when it has no direct edge), and the group's contribution does not move with age, gains or other inputs outside those six indicators. Self-probe: for the typical person the group's contribution is 0.814 at 20 years and 0.814 at 45 years, and 0.814 at 0 US dollars and 0.814 at 20000 US dollars of capital gains; it changes with race, from 0.814 for White to 0.003 for Black. Its largest member by far is the White chain (switching the White chain off moves the training AUC from 0.9099 to 0.9083; switching the whole group off moves it to 0.9074).
ann_131.proposed: Fixed corrections for single categories, led by one for White people; through them a typical person of Asian or Pacific Islander race gets about 32% against about 63% as White.

ann_132.original: The whole model: the parts feed the output node side by side, where their outputs add on the logit scale and a sigmoid turns the sum into the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 a year or less). The explanation reproduces the network to within 6.1e-16 on all 39,073 training rows. On the training split the model's mean predicted chance is 0.762 against an observed rate of 0.761, with AUC 0.9099. Hypothesis: the model is a linear score in the inputs (the direct terms) plus a handful of separate corrections: a youth hinge, a second capital-gains slope above a threshold, an occupation and education gate, and two-valued offsets for single categories; since the parts feed the output in parallel, their effects add on the logit and the parts do not interact. Self-probe of additivity for the typical person: the score is 1.920 and -2.358 at 25 years with 0 US dollars and 10000 US dollars of capital gains, and 0.500 and -3.778 at 45 years: the same change in score from capital gains at both ages, while the change in predicted chance differs (87% to 9% against 62% to 2%) because of the sigmoid. The same holds for race and age: scores 2.233 and 1.920 (Black, White) at the younger age and 0.813 and 0.500 at the older. By ablation the direct terms dominate (training AUC 0.7093 without them), followed by the youth hinge (0.9039) and the single-category group (0.9074); each other part moves the AUC by less than the youth hinge. Because the one-hot inputs are z-scored, rare categories (for example Colombia-born people, private household service) can carry very large shifts from modest weights; these are fitted to few rows.
ann_132.proposed: The model adds a direct sum of every input to switches for large capital gains, youth and most occupations and to corrections for single categories; for a typical person the predicted chance of a low income is about 63%, and capital gains of 6849 US dollars bring it to about 11%.

parts.name: income_model
parts.original_hypothesis: The whole model: the parts feed the output node side by side, where their outputs add on the logit scale and a sigmoid turns the sum into the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 a year or less). The explanation reproduces the network to within 6.1e-16 on all 39,073 training rows. On the training split the model's mean predicted chance is 0.762 against an observed rate of 0.761, with AUC 0.9099. Hypothesis: the model is a linear score in the inputs (the direct terms) plus a handful of separate corrections: a youth hinge, a second capital-gains slope above a threshold, an occupation and education gate, and two-valued offsets for single categories; since the parts feed the output in parallel, their effects add on the logit and the parts do not interact. Self-probe of additivity for the typical person: the score is 1.920 and -2.358 at 25 years with 0 US dollars and 10000 US dollars of capital gains, and 0.500 and -3.778 at 45 years: the same change in score from capital gains at both ages, while the change in predicted chance differs (87% to 9% against 62% to 2%) because of the sigmoid. The same holds for race and age: scores 2.233 and 1.920 (Black, White) at the younger age and 0.813 and 0.500 at the older. By ablation the direct terms dominate (training AUC 0.7093 without them), followed by the youth hinge (0.9039) and the single-category group (0.9074); each other part moves the AUC by less than the youth hinge. Because the one-hot inputs are z-scored, rare categories (for example Colombia-born people, private household service) can carry very large shifts from modest weights; these are fitted to few rows.

parts.name: direct_terms
parts.original_hypothesis: The direct input-to-output edges, gathered in one identity node: a weighted sum of the z-scored inputs (the full sum is attached as analytical_formula evidence; the rounded closed form is off from the exact node by up to 0.034 on a node whose training range spans 38.5). Hypothesis: this linear score carries most of the model's ranking: higher capital gains, capital losses, schooling and weekly hours, and being married, each move the prediction towards a high income in proportion to the input. The heaviest edges per sd are capital gains -2.49, married to a civilian spouse -1.19, not living in a family -0.85, husband -0.75, education-num -0.56, wife -0.56, unmarried -0.54, hours per week -0.31, sex (male) -0.31 and capital losses -0.27. Because the one-hot indicators are z-scored, a category's effect is the difference between two levels' edges, not one weight. Self-probe of linearity for the typical person: the direct sum is -0.983, -1.483 and -1.982 at 20 hours, 40 hours and 60 hours (equal steps), and -0.615, -1.483 and -2.351 at education levels 5 on the 1-16 scale, 9 on the 1-16 scale and 13 on the 1-16 scale; the predicted chance of a low income falls from 80% to 42% over that range. Capital losses lower it too: 63% at 0 US dollars and 31% at 2000 US dollars. Marital status moves it most among the categories: with everything else held at the typical (married, husband) case, setting marital status to never married moves the direct sum from -1.48 to 0.90 and the predicted chance from 63% to 95%. For a never-married person not in a family, being a man lowers the predicted chance from 96% to 92%. Setting the whole direct sum to its training mean drops the training AUC from 0.9099 to 0.7093, by far the largest loss of any part.

parts.name: capital_gain_gate

Hypothesis: once capital gains pass a threshold the model adds a second, steeper push towards a high income on top of the direct capital-gains edge. For the typical person the gate is still shut at 4630 US dollars and open at 4640 US dollars. At 10000 US dollars it adds -0.96 to the logit, so the predicted chance of a low income is 2% with the gate and 6% without it. In the training data it acts on 2094 people (mean contribution -2.51 on the logit for them; their low-income rate is 13.7%). Outside the Portugal-born, the gate is off for 0 people with gains of 4650 dollars or more and on for 0 people with less. The Portugal term is kept because it matters for that group: for a Portugal-born typical person the gate is still shut at 20000 US dollars and opens only by 40000 US dollars; of the 49 Portugal-born training people, 0 have the gate on, and 1 of them has gains above the usual threshold yet keeps it shut. Switching the gate off moves the training AUC from 0.9099 to 0.9093: a small loss, because the direct edge already separates most high earners.

parts.name: young_age_gate
parts.original_hypothesis: A hinge on age with a handlers-or-cleaners term (formula attached as analytical_formula evidence, z units; the rounded closed form is off from the exact node by up to 0.0062). Its output enters the logit with weight 0.67, towards a low income. Hypothesis: the model treats youth as a strong sign of a low income and, past the hinge, almost ignores age. For the typical person the hinge is open at 34 years and shut at 35 years; at 20 years it adds 2.05 to the logit (predicted chance of a low income 93%, against 65% without the hinge). Above the hinge only the direct age edge is left (weight -0.06 per sd), so in the whole model the typical person's predicted chance moves only from 63% at 35 years to 62% at 45 years. Partner: being a handler or cleaner moves the hinge to older ages; for a typical handler or cleaner it is still open at 43 years and shut at 44 years. In the training data the hinge is open for 17,107 people (low-income rate 89.5%, mean contribution 1.25 on the logit for them); it is open for all 14,746 people aged 32 or younger (0 of them have it shut) and for 1310 people aged 34 or older. Switching it off moves the training AUC from 0.9099 to 0.9039, the second-largest loss of any part.

parts.name: occupation_gate
parts.original_hypothesis: A gate over occupation, doctorate, work-without-pay and born-in-Colombia indicators, with two small inner units (formula attached as analytical_formula evidence, z units; the rounded closed form is off from the exact node by up to 0.0058). Its output enters the logit with weight 0.24, towards a low income. Hypothesis: the model gives a fixed push towards a low income to almost everyone, and withholds it from executives or managers, members of the armed forces, farmers or fishers, doctorate holders and people working without pay; being born in Colombia reopens the gate with a very large push. Self-probe over every occupation for the typical person: the gate's output is 1.21 for administrative or clerical work (adding 0.29 to the logit), 1.54 for sales, and 0.0, 0.0 and 0.0 for executive or managerial, armed forces and farming or fishing. A doctorate also shuts it (0.0, against 1.21 for a high-school graduate), and so does working without pay (0.0). For a typical executive born in Colombia the output is 39.2 and the predicted chance of a low income above 99%, against 56% for one born in the United States. In the training data the gate is open for 32,617 people and shut for 6456. Of the 6046 people in the three occupations, 4 have it open, and 4 of those were born in Colombia; of the 473 doctorate holders, 0 have it open; outside the three occupations and the doctorates, 11 people have it shut, and 11 of them work without pay. The Colombia term is fitted to 64 Colombia-born training people: for them the gate adds 10.3 to the logit on average, their mean predicted chance of a low income is 1.000 and their observed rate 98.4%. Switching the gate off moves the training AUC from 0.9099 to 0.9092.

parts.name: single_category_units
parts.original_hypothesis: Composition of six parallel children, added side by side at the output: the White and the Asian or Pacific Islander race chains, the other-service unit, the seventh-to-eighth-grade unit, the Hungary unit and the eleventh-grade unit. Its contribution is the sum of the children's. Hypothesis: each of the six children takes a single category indicator as its entry, so each is a two-valued offset for one category (on the data, a correction to that indicator's direct edge, or the whole of that indicator's effect when it has no direct edge), and the group's contribution does not move with age, gains or other inputs outside those six indicators. Self-probe: for the typical person the group's contribution is 0.814 at 20 years and 0.814 at 45 years, and 0.814 at 0 US dollars and 0.814 at 20000 US dollars of capital gains; it changes with race, from 0.814 for White to 0.003 for Black. Its largest member by far is the White chain (switching the White chain off moves the training AUC from 0.9099 to 0.9083; switching the whole group off moves it to 0.9074).

parts.name: eleventh_grade_unit
parts.original_hypothesis: A unit read from the eleventh-grade education indicator alone (formula attached as analytical_formula evidence, z units; the rounded closed form is off from the exact node by up to 0.00053). Its output enters the logit with weight 0.049, the same direction as the indicator's direct edge (0.017 per sd). The unit never clips: its output is positive on all 39,073 training rows (share 1.0), so on the data it is an affine function of the indicator. Hypothesis: it adds to the direct edge, so the model gives people who left school after eleventh grade an extra push towards a low income beyond what education-num carries. Self-probe for the typical person (education-num held at its typical value): switching the indicator from high-school graduate to eleventh grade moves this unit's contribution from -0.009 to 0.25 and the direct terms from -1.48 to -1.39; the predicted chance of a low income rises from 63% to 71%. Switching the unit to its training mean leaves the training AUC at 0.9099.

closed_form.rounding: weights and biases at 3 significant figures

parts.name: tenth_grade_operator_unit
parts.original_hypothesis: A unit read from the tenth-grade and vocational-associate-degree indicators and the machine-operator indicator (formula attached as analytical_formula evidence, z units; the rounded closed form is off from the exact node by up to 0.0041). Its output enters the logit with weight -0.038, towards a high income. Hypothesis: a small push towards a high income for everyone except machine operators or inspectors, which grows for tenth-grade leavers; machine operators lose it unless they left school after tenth grade. Self-probe for the typical person: the output is 1.84 for a high-school graduate, 6.00 for a tenth-grade leaver (contribution -0.23 on the logit), and for a typical machine operator it is 0.0 as a high-school graduate, 0.0 with a vocational associate degree and 2.10 as a tenth-grade leaver. In the training data the unit is off for 2292 people, and 0 of the off rows are outside machine operation; of the 2417 machine operators, 125 keep it on, and 125 of those left school after tenth grade. Education-num is held at its typical value in these probes, so the tenth-grade case isolates the indicator; education-num's own direct edge is where most of the schooling effect sits. Switching the unit off leaves the training AUC at 0.9099: a negligible part.

parts.name: other_service_unit
parts.original_hypothesis: A unit read from the other-service occupation indicator alone (formula attached as analytical_formula evidence, z units; the rounded closed form is off from the exact node by up to 5.1e-05). Its output enters the logit with weight -0.06, while the same indicator's direct edge weighs 0.30 per sd. Hypothesis: a two-valued lookup that slightly trims the direct push of other-service work towards a low income. Self-probe for the typical person: the unit's output is 1.60 in other service and 0.0 in a professional specialty, adding -0.10 to the logit for the other-service case. In the training data it is on for the 3916 people in other service; 0 of them have it off and 0 other people have it on. Switching it off leaves the training AUC at 0.9099 (with it, 0.9099): a negligible part.

parts.name: hungary_unit
parts.original_hypothesis: A unit read from the born-in-Hungary indicator alone (formula attached as analytical_formula evidence, z units; the rounded closed form is off from the exact node by up to 0.0026). Its output enters the logit with weight -0.0056; the indicator has no direct edge. Hypothesis: a two-valued lookup fitted to 16 Hungary-born training people that gives them a small push towards a high income. Self-probe for the typical person: the unit's output is 48.8 for a Hungary-born and 0.0 for a United-States-born case, adding -0.27 to the logit (predicted chance of a low income 57% against 63%). The large output on a tiny weight comes from z-scoring a rare indicator. In the training data it is on for the 16 Hungary-born people; 0 of them have it off and 0 others have it on. Switching it off leaves the training AUC at 0.9099.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient); an input the data ties to a category takes its typical value within that category (linked inputs)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording

ann_119.text: This part acts on 2094 of 39073 training people (5%).
For a typical person it acts on, it slightly lowers the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) from about 4% without this part to about 2% with it.
In the training data, 287 of these 2094 people had a low income ($50,000 or less).

A higher capital gains slightly lowers the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less), and even more so if country of birth is something other than Portugal (slowly at first, then faster for people with country of birth other than Portugal): for a typical person, capital gains going from 0 US dollars to 6849 US dollars moves the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) from about 63% to about 11% if country of birth is something other than Portugal, and from about 63% to about 15% if the country of birth is Portugal.

Through this part, the model treats a higher capital gains as clearly lowering the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) with nothing until about 4507 US dollars, then steadily: for a typical person, it goes from about 63% at 0 US dollars to about 54% at 6849 US dollars.

Through this part, for a typical person this part acts on, the model gives a slightly higher predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) if the country of birth is Portugal (about 4%) than if country of birth is something other than Portugal (about 2%).

ann_120.text: This part acts on 17107 of 39073 training people (44%).
For a typical person it acts on, it slightly raises the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) from above 99% without this part to above 99% with it.
In the training data, 15305 of these 17107 people had a low income ($50,000 or less).

Through this part, age clearly lowers the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) while it stays below about 34 years (for 1683 of the 39073 training people it already changes above that): for a typical such person, going from 19 years to 90 years moves it from about 94% to about 63%.
Other effects: a higher age lowers it steadily up to about 34 years, then no further; handlers or cleaners (rather than any other occupation) raises it (on the training data only).
Smaller effects, each changing the predicted value only slightly: age depending on occupation lowers it in an uneven way.

Smaller effects, each changing the predicted value only slightly: country of birth depending on occupation raises it; sales (rather than any other occupation) raises it; occupation depending on highest education raises it. The model has little data on some of these: only 12 training people (armed forces).

summary.text: The model treats a higher capital gains as clearly lowering the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) slowly at first, then faster: for a typical person, it goes from about 63% at 0 US dollars to about 11% at 6849 US dollars, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted risk cannot go much lower.

For a typical person, the model gives a clearly lower predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) if the highest education is professional school degree (with education level (1 = preschool to 16 = doctorate) at 15 on the 1-16 scale, as in the data) (about 19%) than if highest education is something other than 10th grade, 11th grade, doctorate, master's degree, preschool, professional school degree, some college, 7th-8th grade, 9th grade, associate degree (academic), associate degree (vocational), bachelor's degree (about 63%).

The model treats a higher education level as clearly lowering the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) in an uneven way: for a typical person, it goes from about 79% at 7 on the 1-16 scale to about 35% at 13 on the 1-16 scale (with highest education at bachelor's degree, as in the data).

For a typical person, going from country of birth other than Colombia to Colombia moves the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) from about 63% to above 99% if highest education is something other than doctorate, and from about 22% to above 99% if the highest education is doctorate (with education level (1 = preschool to 16 = doctorate) at 16 on the 1-16 scale, as in the data).

Through one part of the model, age clearly lowers the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) while it stays below about 34 years (for 1683 of the 39073 training people it already changes above that): for a typical such person, going from 19 years to 90 years moves it from about 94% to about 63%.
